what_it_does: Private Set Intersection (PSI) is a cryptographic technique that lets two parties figure out which items they have in common without either side revealing anything else from their lists — useful, for example, when two hospitals want to find shared patients without exposing their full databases. One way to make PSI provably secure is to use Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE), which lets a computer perform calculations directly on encrypted data without ever decrypting it; the catch is that FHE is enormously slow. Ares is a hardware accelerator built on an FPGA (a reprogrammable chip) that is co-designed with the PSI software to overcome this slowness. Its main trick, called Lazy Relinearization, postpones an expensive re-encoding step that standard FHE requires after every multiplication, eliminating many redundant operations specific to the PSI computation pattern. The result is claimed to be much higher throughput and better use of the chip's memory bandwidth than general-purpose FHE accelerators provide.
